parts.text:
You are a requirements analyst at the start of a software project. Nobody has designed the service yet. Attached are the full transcripts of three interviews with its future users: a fleet technician, a dispatcher, and the platform's airspace desk. The transcripts are everything you know about these users and their world.

Write user stories from the interviews. Each story:

- is told from one user's point of view, in that user's language;
- says what happened or what situation the user is in, what they need, and what they fear will happen without it;
- describes outcomes the user cares about, not procedures, screens, or steps;
- contains no numbers that the user would not naturally say, no technical terms, no names of technologies, and no proposals for how the service should work inside;
- is three to eight sentences long;
- rests on what the interviews say; where a story rests on an assumption the interviews do not settle, state the assumption in one sentence.

Write stories for ordinary days and for bad days. Where users would disagree with each other, write both stories; do not resolve the conflict. Aim for forty to sixty stories. Prefer more distinct situations over more variations of one situation.

Output the stories as YAML in exactly this format:

```yaml
- id: US-01
  user: dispatcher            # fleet technician | dispatcher | airspace desk
  title: short title in the user's words
  story: >
    ...
  fear: >
    what goes wrong for this user if the need is not met
  assumption: null            # or one sentence
  interview_ref: dispatcher, worst day
```

After the stories, list every question you would still ask these users or the people who run their business, if you could. Do not wait for answers.

# Interview — a fleet technician

**Interviewer:** Could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you, from the moment you start until you finish?

**Interviewee:** Well, I usually start by checking which drones have been flagged overnight for maintenance or came back with faults from their runs. Then I head out to our sites to swap out batteries, fix landing gear, or pull birds out of service that need proper bench repairs in the workshop. 

A big part of the day is also setting up new charging pads and getting fresh birds added to our fleet registry so they're ready to fly. Sometimes I'm dealing with different connector types depending on the drone model, so I have to make sure I've got the right spares in the van. 

By the afternoon, I'm usually finishing up paperwork for the regulators, since we have to show how every single drone and pad has been looked after if they ask.

**Interviewer:** Could you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

**Interviewee:** That has to be a couple of weeks ago when a cold front blew in right when we had a batch of drones out on inspections and hospital runs. The freezing wind drained their batteries way faster than expected, and we had birds trying to squeeze onto our charging pads all at once. 

To top it all off, the radio links were dropping out because of the weather, so status reports were coming in late or completely out of order. I spent the whole day rushing between sites trying to clear jammed charging connectors and manually pulling dying drones out of service before they caused a pile-up.

**Interviewer:** Right after something goes wrong like that—say, a drone drops out or a pad jams during a crisis—what are the very first things you need to know?

**Interviewee:** I need to know right away which specific drone is acting up, exactly which site and pad it's sitting on, and what the mechanical fault is so I know what tools to grab. 

Since our radio links can be flaky—especially in bad weather—I also need to figure out if the status report I'm looking at is actually current or if it's an old message arriving late.

**Interviewer:** Is there anything you check by hand yourself today because you don't trust what the system tells you?

**Interviewee:** I always check the charging connector and the battery on the bird myself with my own eyes and hands. You can't just trust a screen when a connector is fried or caked in grime from a site near the port, and I need to know for sure whether it's safe to handle.

**Interviewer:** When you're out doing your work, who do you hand tasks or information over to, and who hands things over to you?

**Interviewee:** I don't really hand tasks over to other people in a formal way. Management lets me know which new drones need to be added to the fleet or which ones are retiring, and I just get on with the physical work on the birds and the pads. 

If something goes wrong with a flight or a customer needs an update, our company's own systems handle reaching out to the right people—that's not my job. My focus is entirely on keeping the hardware in working order and making sure our maintenance records are straight for the regulators.

**Interviewer:** What are you most afraid a new service might do wrong in your day-to-day work?

**Interviewee:** I'm mostly afraid that a new service might mess up our maintenance records or drop the history of what we've done to a drone. If the regulators ask us to prove how a bird was looked after and the records are scrambled or missing because of a software glitch, we're in serious trouble. 

I also worry that any new system might start sending duplicate instructions or glitch out when the radio links are already patchy, which just makes more physical work for me out in the field.


---

# Interview — a dispatcher

**Interviewer:** Could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you, from the moment you start until you log off?

**Interviewee:** When I start my shift, I check what jobs are lined up for the day—whether that's parcel deliveries, medical logistics for the hospital, or infrastructure checks. Since I'm legally responsible for the flights, I spend a lot of time looking at which drones we have ready, checking their batteries, sensors, and making sure I pick the right machine for the weight and distance. 

The airspace is always shifting with new closures from the authorities, so I have to keep a close eye on those zones and make sure our corridors stay clear. Throughout the day, I'm signing off on flight plans, watching the automated flights make their way between sites, and dealing with real-world surprises like a load not being ready on time or sudden wind draining batteries faster than expected. 

It gets pretty hectic when multiple dispatchers are trying to book the same busy launch pads or popular drones at the same time. By the end of the day, I'm just making sure everything has landed safely back at our charging pads and handling any last-minute route adjustments before logging off.

**Interviewer:** You mentioned it gets pretty hectic when multiple dispatchers are trying to book the same busy launch pads or popular drones at the same time; could you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months and what made it so bad?

**Interviewee:** That would have to be the day a sudden airspace closure came down right in the middle of our busiest afternoon, forcing multiple drones to change course while our radio links were acting up. On top of that, we had several dispatchers all scrambling for the few available take-off pads at our main site to get birds safely down. 

What made it really stressful was that the status reports from the drones were arriving late and out of order because of patchy coverage, so I couldn't tell right away if my override instructions had actually reached them. You just hold your breath and hope everything sorts itself out on the autopilots while you try to untangle the landing schedule.

**Interviewer:** When things like that happen—or right after something has gone wrong—what are the very first things you need to know, and where do you look to find that information?

**Interviewee:** The very first thing I need to know is whether our drones are safely clear of any sudden airspace closures and if they're still following their corridors. I also need to check which charging pads are actually free right now so I know where we can bring them down. 

To find that, I look at our current map and status screens to see where the birds actually are and what the authorities have just announced. But with the radios being patchy, I've learned I can't always trust the latest report on the screen to match what the drone is doing out there.

**Interviewer:** That leads right into something I wanted to ask about: what are the specific things you find yourself checking by hand today because you simply don't trust what the system tells you?

**Interviewee:** I find myself double-checking whether a drone actually received an instruction, because our links are so unreliable that commands can get sent twice or not at all. I also have to manually verify the battery levels on our drones before signing off a flight, especially when it's cold and windy, because those drain much faster than the standard plans account for. 

And when status reports arrive late, out of order, or not at all, I just have to look at where the bird was supposed to be and guess its actual state until the radios catch up.

**Interviewer:** Who do you hand your completed work or ongoing tasks over to at the end of your shift, and who hands work to you when you start?

**Interviewee:** I don't really hand tasks over to a specific person when I leave, because we all just share the same shift load and keep an eye on whatever is currently flying. When I start, I don't get a handoff from anyone either; I just sit down, look at what jobs are waiting in the queue, and start checking which drones and sites are ready to go.

**Interviewer:** What are you most afraid that a new service or system would get wrong in your day-to-day work?

**Interviewee:** I'm most afraid that the system might try to automatically pick a drone or plan a route for me, which goes against our policy because I'm the one legally responsible for the flight. I'm also really worried it might lock up or crash during a busy moment, or fail to handle those delayed and out-of-order status reports properly when the radios act up.


---

# Interview — a member of the platform's airspace desk

**Interviewer:** Could you walk me through what an ordinary working day looks like for you, from the moment you start your shift until you log off?

**Interviewee:** An ordinary day starts with me logging on to check the shared airspace picture, making sure all the corridors between the named sites and the current zones are up to date. My main job is keeping track of what the authorities put out, like planned closures with their start and end times, or sudden ones that drop on us right away. 

Throughout the shift, I spend a lot of time updating those closures when the authorities change them—like when they widen an area or push back an end time while drones from our different customers, like the parcel delivery or hospital logistics firms, are already up in the air. When a closure comes down, I need to see how much disruption it actually caused across those companies. 

Every now and then, the server we run on gets restarted or drops out for a few minutes while things are flying, so I just keep an eye on things until it's back up. We don't steer drones or handle routes here, so it's really about maintaining that common map and dealing with the authorities' changes until my shift ends and I log off.

**Interviewer:** Could you tell me about the worst day you've had in the last few months, and what made it so bad?

**Interviewee:** The worst days are when the authorities drop a sudden closure right in the middle of the day, and then keep shifting the boundaries and extending the end times while our customers' drones are already out flying in the corridors. What makes it so stressful is scrambling to update our map while trying to figure out just how badly the new shape of the closure disrupted everyone all at once. To top it off, sometimes the server decides to crash or restart right in the thick of all that chaos, leaving us blind for a few minutes while we just have to wait for it to come back up.

**Interviewer:** When the server drops out and leaves you blind like that, what is the very first thing you need to know or check the moment it comes back up?

**Interviewee:** The first thing I need to check is whether the active closures and the flight corridors are still showing what they were before the server went down, especially if the authorities sent out any updates while we were offline. I need to make sure the picture matches reality so we aren't missing a sudden change or an amended end time while drones are still out there flying.

**Interviewer:** Is there anything you find yourself having to check by hand today because you don't fully trust the system?

**Interviewee:** I mostly have to check by hand how much disruption a closure actually caused across our different customers once the authorities finish changing it. The system doesn't really give me a clear picture of the overall impact on everyone's flights, so I'm left trying to piece that together myself while things are moving.

**Interviewer:** When you hand your work off to someone else at the end of your shift, or when someone hands work to you, who are you passing things to or receiving them from?

**Interviewee:** I'm handing things off to whoever is taking over the next shift here on the airspace desk. We don't deal with the customer companies' internal staff or their management when passing over the work—it's just a handoff between us desk folks who keep an eye on the shared airspace picture.

**Interviewer:** What are you most afraid a new service or system would do wrong in your daily work?

**Interviewee:** I'm really afraid a new system would try to do too much, like adding dashboards, reports, or automatic alerts that we don't need and our companies don't want. I'm also worried it might get bogged down trying to handle corporate logins or route planning, which just gets in the way of keeping our basic map and closures accurate.
